newsitem.title: UK: UK's Lilley sees average pension fund 130,000 stg.
newsitem.headline: UK's Lilley sees average pension fund 130,000 stg.

text.p: British Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley said under the Conservative government's proposed new pension scheme, a worker on average earnings would build up a retirement fund worth 130,000 stg after making the minimum contributions over their working life. This would provide a pension of 175 stg per week at today's prices, he told a news conference.
Workers and employers would be encouraged to save more than the minimum in their fund.
Lilley said the new system would be phased in gradually over a generation. Existing pensioners would not be affected and would continue to receive their state pensions.
The current working generation would continue to build entitlements to the basic state pension and were free to remain in or opt out of SERPS (State Earnings-Related Pension Scheme).
"The impact on public revenues of the rebates needed to fund investment would grow very graudally over 40 years," Lilley said.

In future, pension contributions would be paid out of net, taxed income and all pension income would be entirely tax-free. This is the reverse of the present system, under which pension contributions attract tax relief but pensions are taxed.
Lilley said pension providers would be invited to join a working party which would draw up detailed proposals.
The government aimed to delevop a simple but effective regulatory regime.
"The past abuse of mis-selling personal pensions to those who did not need them cannot recur under this proposal since everyone will need and get a Basic Pension Plus fund."
Lilley said the impact on public finances would be quite manageable.
"The net value of extra investment will mount at only about 160 million stg a year and eventually it will produce massive savings in public expenditure, reaching 40 billion stg a year.

"At its peak the net revenue foregone will be less than the peak cost of SERPS rebates, which we have already taken in our stride...The extra rebates are small relative to normal growth of tax revenues," Lilley said.
